questions.stem: When and where is The One Day of the Year set?
options: Around Anzac Day in the late 1950s, in the Cook family's Sydney home
Around Australia Day in the 1930s, in a country pub run by Alf Cook
During the Second World War, in an army training camp near Sydney
Around Anzac Day in the late 1950s, in the Cook family's Melbourne home
questions.explanation: The play takes place in the Cooks' small working-class house in Sydney in the late 1950s, before, on and after Anzac Day. Keeping the action in one home turns a national argument into a family one.

questions.stem: What do Hughie and his girlfriend Jan plan to do on Anzac Day?
options: Join a student protest against the march outside the Cenotaph
Cover the day's heavy drinking for the university newspaper
March with Alf and Wacka in the Anzac Day parade in the city
Cover the solemn dawn service for the university newspaper
questions.explanation: Hughie and Jan want to show the 'real' Anzac Day: the drunkenness of the afternoon, not the solemn dawn. Their plan sets up the clash with Alf.

questions.stem: What does Hughie refuse to do, for the first time, this Anzac Day?
options: Watch the march on television at home
Lend his camera to Jan for her article
Help his mother prepare the family lunch
Go to the dawn service with his father
questions.explanation: Going to the dawn service with Alf has been their routine for years. Hughie's refusal is the first open sign that he rejects what the day means to his father.

questions.stem: Late on Anzac Day, Wacka finally talks at length to Dot. What does he describe?
options: The Gallipoli landing, and how hollow the fame that followed felt
His pride in leading the city march as the oldest digger that morning
The glory of the landing, and how proud the fame made the men feel
His years fighting beside Alf in the Second World War overseas
questions.explanation: Wacka, who says little for most of the play, describes the confusion and horror of Gallipoli. He treats the fame of the Anzacs as something the public made, not something the men felt. His war was Gallipoli, not Alf's Second World War.

questions.stem: In what state does Alf come home at the end of Anzac Day?
options: Injured after a fight with police during the march
Ashamed and apologetic, wishing he had stayed home
Drunk and dishevelled, full of stories from the pub
Sober and silent, refusing to talk about his day
questions.explanation: Alf returns drunk from a day at the pub. For Hughie this seems to prove his case about the day, which makes the argument between them far more bitter.

questions.stem: What brings the conflict to a head in the final act?
options: Jan's father complains to Alf about the way Hughie has behaved
Wacka repeats to Alf what Hughie said about the diggers that day
Alf loses his job as a result of what he did on Anzac Day
Alf sees the article about Anzac Day in the university newspaper
questions.explanation: Days after Anzac Day the article appears, and Alf reads it as an attack on the diggers and on himself. Father and son have it out at last.

questions.stem: How is the conflict between Alf and Hughie left at the end of the play?
options: They reach an uneasy truce, though Hughie still rejects how the day is kept
Alf wins the argument, and Hughie apologises for writing the article
Alf comes round to Hughie's view and agrees the day should change
Father and son stay estranged, with no move toward reconciliation
questions.explanation: Father and son argue but move toward reconciliation. Hughie does not take back his view of the day, so the ending settles the family conflict without settling the argument about Anzac Day.

questions.stem: What is Alf Cook's job?
options: He works as a tram conductor
He works as a lift driver
He works as an engineer
He works as a publican
questions.explanation: Alf drives a lift and feels he has never got anywhere; he never became the engineer he might have been. His low-status job helps explain why Anzac Day means so much to him.

questions.stem: In which war did Alf fight?
options: The First World War, at Gallipoli
The Korean War
The Vietnam War
The Second World War
questions.explanation: Alf is a veteran of the Second World War. Wacka, his older mate, is the one who was at Gallipoli in the First World War.

questions.stem: Who is Wacka Dawson?
options: Dot's brother, who runs the hotel near the Cooks' home
Alf's quiet mate, an old soldier who was at Gallipoli
Jan's father, a wealthy lawyer from the North Shore
Hughie's lecturer, who edits the student newspaper
questions.explanation: Wacka is a Gallipoli veteran and a friend of the family. He is gentle and mostly silent, which makes his late speech about the war all the more powerful.

questions.stem: Jan Castle differs from the Cooks mainly because she:
options: is a mature-age student who works nights to pay fees
has left university to work as a typist in a city office
comes from a wealthy family on Sydney's North Shore
has recently migrated to Sydney from the north of England
questions.explanation: Jan is a university student from a well-off North Shore family. Her presence brings class into the argument: Alf feels she looks down on people like him.

questions.stem: Which statement best describes Dot (Mum)?
options: Quiet and timid, she rarely challenges her husband's views
Sentimental about Anzac Day, she sides with Alf against Hughie
Cold and distant, she sides with Jan against her own family
Practical and sharp-tongued, she argues with both Alf and Hughie
questions.explanation: Dot holds the family together. She tells Alf and Hughie both what she thinks, and she is the one Wacka finally confides in about Gallipoli.

questions.stem: Why does Anzac Day matter so much to Alf in particular?
options: It is the one day he can share his own war stories with his son
It is the day he feels closest to the officers he once served under
It is the one day he feels respected, in a life he feels has gone nowhere
It is the day he was given a medal for bravery in front of the whole city
questions.explanation: Alf resents his job and the people who look down on him. On Anzac Day he is a digger among diggers, so an attack on the day feels like an attack on his worth.

questions.stem: How does Dot feel about Hughie's education?
options: Indifferent to it, since she rarely asks what he is studying
Worried that it will draw him into dangerous radical politics
Proud of it, but hurt that it seems to make him look down on her
Opposed to it, because she thinks a university is a waste of money
questions.explanation: The Cooks have worked to give Hughie the education they never had. Dot fears the result is a son who sees her as nothing, which shows the cost of social mobility.

questions.stem: How does Wacka's attitude to the war differ from Alf's?
options: Wacka boasts about it at any chance; Alf would rather forget it
Wacka thinks the war was justified; Alf now thinks it was a terrible mistake
Wacka shares Hughie's contempt for the day; Alf is unsure what to think
Wacka rarely speaks of it and sees little glory in it; Alf celebrates it loudly
questions.explanation: Wacka, the real Anzac, is modest and unsentimental about Gallipoli. Alf's loud celebration contrasts with Wacka's silence, which complicates both Alf's and Hughie's views of the day.

questions.stem: What inspired Seymour to write the play?
options: A speech by the Prime Minister at the opening of a war memorial
A letter Seymour received from the widow of a Gallipoli veteran
A newspaper report of a riot during an Adelaide Anzac Day march
An article in a Sydney University student paper criticising Anzac Day
questions.explanation: Seymour drew on an article in Honi Soit, the University of Sydney's student newspaper, that criticised Anzac Day. Hughie and Jan's article echoes it.

questions.stem: What happened when the play was offered to the 1960 Adelaide Festival of Arts?
options: It won the festival's top prize
It opened the festival in the city
It was closed by police on opening night
The festival's board rejected it
questions.explanation: The festival's board turned the play down because its view of Anzac Day was seen as too controversial. It was first performed by an amateur Adelaide company later in 1960.

questions.stem: Alf complains about 'Poms' and newly arrived migrants. What context does this reflect?
options: The abolition of the White Australia policy in the late 1950s
Soldiers returning from Korea and competing with locals for jobs
Britain's decision to stop sending its migrants to Australia
Large-scale migration after the Second World War, which changed 1950s Australia
questions.explanation: Post-war migration from Britain and Europe, including Italy, was changing Australian society. Alf's grumbling shows a working man who feels his country slipping away from him. The White Australia policy was still in place, not dismantled until the following decades.

questions.stem: Why was the play controversial when it was first staged?
options: It showed soldiers drinking on stage, which theatres were then banned from doing
It claimed that the Gallipoli landing had been invented by newspapers
It mocked the royal family at a time when the Queen was visiting Australia
It questioned how Anzac Day was kept, when many treated the day as sacred
questions.explanation: By the late 1950s Anzac Day was close to untouchable. A play showing the drinking, and a young man rejecting the day, provoked strong reactions from returned servicemen and others.

questions.stem: Which social change of the 1950s does Hughie represent?
options: Young men being conscripted to fight in a war in South-East Asia
Women entering the paid workforce in large numbers after the war
Young people leaving Australia to find work in Britain
Working-class children reaching university for the first time
questions.explanation: Hughie is the first in his family to go to university. His education opens a gap between him and his parents, in ideas, in language and in class.

questions.stem: Which conflict is at the centre of the play?
options: A clash between generations over what Anzac Day means
A clash between Alf and Wacka over how to remember Gallipoli
A struggle between unions and bosses over higher wages
A feud between the Cooks and Jan's parents over the couple
questions.explanation: The father-son conflict carries a national argument: whether Anzac Day honours sacrifice or has become an excuse to get drunk. Both sides are given real force.

questions.stem: How does the play present mateship?
options: As a mask for drunkenness that the play condemns
As a bond Alf shares with the officers he served under
As real and loyal, as when Alf fiercely defends Wacka
As a myth, since Alf secretly despises Wacka's weakness
questions.explanation: Alf turns on anyone who insults his mate, and his loyalty to Wacka is one of his best qualities. The play does not mock mateship, even while it questions the day built around it.

questions.stem: The play suggests that Alf's loud nationalism partly comes from:
options: his high rank as an officer in the army during the Second World War
his time at Gallipoli, which left him bitter towards Britain
his sense of being looked down on because of his work and class
his English upbringing, which he tries hard to hide from others
questions.explanation: Alf complains about people who treat him like dirt. His pride in being Australian, and in Anzac Day, gives him a dignity his job does not. He fought in the Second World War, not at Gallipoli.

questions.stem: Which question about remembering war does the play leave open?
options: Whether the Gallipoli campaign was planned by British or Australian generals
Whether Gallipoli veterans deserve more honour than later soldiers
Whether Anzac Day honours the dead or has become an excuse for drinking
Whether Australia should have fought in the Second World War
questions.explanation: Hughie sees a drunken ritual; Alf sees a sacred day; Wacka sees something more complicated than either. Seymour lets the audience weigh them rather than giving a verdict.

questions.stem: The play takes place almost entirely inside the Cooks' house. What is the effect?
options: It allows the play to show many different suburbs and social classes
It shows off the Cooks' prosperity, as the house is large and comfortable
It keeps a national debate inside one family, so it feels personal
It lets the audience follow the whole march as it moves through the city
questions.explanation: The march and the pubs happen offstage. What the audience sees is their effect on one family's kitchen, lounge and bedroom, which makes the argument intimate.

questions.stem: Hughie's room is a glassed-in sleep-out with university pennants on the wall. What does this suggest?
options: He is the most important person in the house, as his room is the largest
He has been sent outside as a punishment for refusing the dawn service
He has cut himself off from the family and no longer eats or talks with them
He is part of the family home but already living in a different world
questions.explanation: The sleep-out is attached to the house but set apart from the kitchen where his parents and Wacka gather. The pennants mark his new university world.

questions.stem: How does Seymour use language to separate the generations?
options: Alf and Dot speak broad Australian vernacular, while Hughie uses university words
Alf speaks very formally, while Hughie uses broad Australian slang throughout
Wacka speaks most fluently, with the longest speeches from the start
Jan adopts broad vernacular to fit in, while Hughie mocks her for it
questions.explanation: Alf's 'bloody', 'grog' and 'awright' sit beside Hughie's talk of theory and the proletariat. The gap in their language shows how education has divided the family.

questions.stem: Why is it dramatically powerful that Wacka speaks about Gallipoli only late in the play?
options: It shows that he has finally come round to Alf's view of the day
It lets him correct Hughie's article before it goes to the printer
It reveals that he was never at Gallipoli and made up his stories
His long silence makes his plain, unheroic account carry great weight
questions.explanation: Everyone else talks about Anzac; Wacka, who was there, says almost nothing. When he finally speaks, his account cuts through both Alf's celebration and Hughie's contempt.

questions.stem: Alf kneels to clean Hughie's shoes while Hughie studies. What does the action suggest?
options: Alf's sacrifice for his son's education, and how it raises Hughie above him
Alf's army habit of neatness, which he forces on everyone in the family
Alf's control over Hughie, whom he still treats as a small child
Alf's eagerness to get Hughie ready for the next dawn service
questions.explanation: The father literally kneels at his son's feet so that the son can study. The image shows both Alf's love and the class gap that education is opening between them.

questions.stem: Who says, 'I'm a bloody Australian and I'll always stand up for bloody Australia.'?
options: Wacka, describing Gallipoli to Dot
Jan, arguing with Alf about the march
Alf, in the opening lines of the play
Hughie, defending his article to Jan
questions.explanation: The play opens with Alf's blunt, swearing patriotism. It establishes at once his pride, his anger and the vernacular voice of the older generation.

questions.stem: Wacka says, 'When we went in there we was nobody. When we come out we was famous.' What does this show?
options: He sees Anzac fame as something the public made, not something the men lived
He still enjoys the attention that he receives from the crowds each Anzac Day
He is proud that the Anzacs earned their fame through their bravery at the landing
He regrets enlisting and blames Alf's generation for the way war is remembered
questions.explanation: Wacka's flat, ungrammatical words cut the legend down to size. In the same speech he calls the fame 'Ballyhoo' and 'Not worth a crumpet'.

questions.stem: Hughie argues that war is so ugly it should be forgotten once it is over. Whose devotion to Anzac Day is he mainly challenging?
options: His mother Dot's, who cooks the family's Anzac lunch
Wacka's, who insists on marching at the very front
Jan's, who wants their article to praise the day
His father Alf's, who sees remembering as a sacred duty
questions.explanation: Hughie's challenge is aimed at Alf, for whom Anzac Day is beyond question. Alf cannot understand how anyone could see remembering as shameful.

questions.stem: Alf replies, 'Ashamed? Ashamed? To fight for your country?' What does this show?
options: His secret shame about his own part in the war, which he has hidden from Dot
His agreement with Hughie that the war should now be quietly forgotten
His fear that Hughie will be called up to fight in the next war overseas
His outrage at the idea that war service could be anything but honourable
questions.explanation: The repeated question shows Alf's disbelief. To him, honouring war service is beyond argument, which is exactly what Hughie is questioning.

questions.stem: Alf tells Dot, 'That's men like my father he's talking about.' What does this reveal?
options: He takes Hughie's attack on the diggers as an attack on his own family
He admits that his father never fought and invented his war stories
He agrees that some diggers disgrace the day with their drinking
He wants Hughie to show more respect to Wacka in particular
questions.explanation: For Alf the diggers are not an abstract idea but his own father and mates. That is why Hughie's criticism feels to him like a betrayal of the family itself.

questions.stem: Watching the marchers, Hughie tells Jan they are 'sort of proud' but 'Not military. Not aggressive.' What does this show?
options: He sees the marchers as aggressive militarists who glorify war and violence
He is mocking the marchers to impress Jan, whom he knows despises them
He has changed his mind and wants to join the march with Alf after all
He sees something dignified in the marchers despite his criticism of the day
questions.explanation: Hughie is torn: he rejects the drinking and the myth, yet is moved by the ordinary men marching. His mixed feelings make him more than a simple rebel.

questions.stem: Dot says Hughie 'looks at me sometimes as though I'm nothing'. What fear does this express?
options: That he plans to marry Jan without telling Alf and Dot first
That he has stopped studying and wasted the money they saved
That his education has taught him to look down on his own parents
That he spends so much time with Jan that his studies suffer
questions.explanation: Dot's words show the personal cost of the education the Cooks worked for. Class, not just Anzac Day, is part of what divides the family.

questions.stem: Which is the strongest topic sentence for the prompt 'The conflict between Alf and Hughie is really about class.' Discuss.
options: The One Day of the Year is a famous Australian play that was first performed in Adelaide in 1960
Seymour suggests that Hughie's education has opened a class gap that sharpens every argument about Anzac Day
In The One Day of the Year, Alf Cook works as a lift driver while his son Hughie is a student at the university
This essay will discuss how class is shown in the play The One Day of the Year by Alan Seymour
questions.explanation: A strong topic sentence takes a position on the prompt and names what the paragraph will prove. The others retell, announce or state facts without arguing.

questions.stem: A student writes: 'Wacka doesn't say much for most of the play.' How could this be turned into analysis?
options: List the scenes in which Wacka appears and the few lines that he speaks
Describe what Wacka wears and where he sits in the Cooks' kitchen
Explain how his silence contrasts with Alf's noise and gives his late speech its force
Add Wacka's age, his unit, and the name of the troopship that carried him to Gallipoli
questions.explanation: Analysis explains what a detail suggests. Linking Wacka's silence to the play's questions about who really owns the Anzac story turns description into argument.
